papers.title: Protein Language Models Improve Quantum Annealing-Based Protein Sequence Search
papers.abstract: By combining protein sequence representations from a pretrained protein language model with a binary variational autoencoder, the researchers improved the accuracy of encoding protein variants into 64 binary variables and reconstructing their amino acid sequences. Using a real D-Wave Advantage System 6 quantum annealer, the researchers optimized three protein sequence design tasks and generated more novel candidates with high computational scores than the conventional method. For AAV capsid variants, the number of candidates exceeding the predefined score threshold increased from 19 with the conventional bVAE to 2,761 with the hyperparameter-optimized pLM-bVAE. However, these results were based on computational predictions and did not experimentally establish improved protein function or a quantum computational advantage. [Quantum Biology Society] One of the greatest challenges in protein design is the enormous number of possible amino acid combinations. Even changing a small number of residues can rapidly expand the sequence space that researchers must explore. Quantum annealing (QA) is one approach to solving such combinatorial optimization problems. However, applying it to protein design presents a fundamental challenge: amino acid sequences must first be converted into binary variables consisting of zeros and ones, which can be processed by a quantum annealer. If this conversion loses important information about how protein sequences are related, even an extensive computational search may fail to identify useful protein candidates. A research team from Kitasato University, RIKEN, the University of Tokyo, Tohoku University, the National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS), and the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) in Japan proposed an artificial intelligence-based binary representation method to address this challenge. The researchers, Hiromi H. Ueda, Andrejs Tučs, Koji Tsuda, Mitsuo Umetsu, and Yutaka Saito, developed pLM-bVAE, a model combining a pretrained protein language model with a binary variational autoencoder. They then evaluated its performance in protein sequence optimization using a D-Wave quantum annealer. Yutaka Saito served as the corresponding author. The study was posted to bioRxiv on November 6, 2026, as a preprint that has not yet undergone peer review. ■ Encoding Protein Sequence Information into 64 Binary Variables Previous approaches to quantum annealing-based protein design have used binary variational autoencoders (bVAEs) to convert amino acid sequences into binary representations. A bVAE consists of two principal components. The encoder compresses an amino acid sequence into a shorter binary vector containing zeros and ones. The decoder then reconstructs an amino acid sequence from the binary vector produced or optimized during computation. This process can be compared to representing locations on a map using compact coordinates. However, the important requirement is not simply to reduce the size of the representation. Sequences that are biologically or evolutionarily related should ideally retain meaningful relationships within the compressed binary space. If similar protein sequences become arbitrarily separated in the binary representation, the optimization algorithm may struggle to explore the sequence space effectively. To improve this mapping, the researchers introduced a protein language model (pLM) before the conventional bVAE architecture. Protein language models are artificial intelligence systems pretrained on large collections of amino acid sequences. They learn statistical patterns associated with amino acid context, sequence relationships, and evolutionary information. The principal model used in the study was ESM2_650M, which contains approximately 650 million parameters. The researchers used this model to generate residue-level representations of protein sequences. These representations were then provided to the bVAE, which converted them into 64-dimensional binary vectors and reconstructed the corresponding amino acid sequences. Importantly, the pretrained protein language model was not further trained during this process. Its parameters were frozen, while the bVAE component was trained to generate binary representations and reconstruct sequences. The optimization also focused on designated variant regions rather than necessarily redesigning an entire protein. The researchers evaluated the method using three publicly available protein variant datasets. The first contained 12,160 peptides with experimentally measured binding affinities to the HLA-A*02:01 major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecule. Levenshtein distance describes the minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions required to transform one sequence into another. BLOSUM62 is an amino acid substitution matrix commonly used to evaluate sequence similarity while accounting for evolutionary relationships. A smaller Levenshtein distance between the original and reconstructed sequences indicates more accurate reconstruction. The researchers also examined whether differences between amino acid sequences were reflected in their binary representations. To do this, they compared pairwise Levenshtein distances between protein sequences with Hamming distances between their corresponding binary vectors. However, the results do not imply that the 64-bit representation captures every structural or functional property of a protein. The predictors were trained using experimentally measured values available in the original public datasets. However, when new sequences were generated during optimization, their scores were calculated by these trained predictors rather than measured experimentally. papers.title: CV-SPINN: complex-valued spin physics-informed neural network for quantum simulation
papers.abstract: Spins are among the most promising qubits because they offer long coherence times, high controllability, and direct readout, enabling applications in quantum sensing, quantum simulation, and quantum information processing. However, numerically simulating and experimentally determining quantum states, particularly in multi-spin systems, remains challenging due to scaling limitations and error accumulation. We introduce CV-SPINN, a complex-valued physics-informed neural network that learns a one-step density-matrix propagator while enforcing Liouville–von Neumann consistency and density-matrix structure (Hermiticity and trace/purity constraints). We show on experiments of simulated cross polarization in systems of two and three spins that CV-SPINN consistently outperforms both baselines based on recent literature (77% – 98% decrease in the mean squared error of the density matrix) and similar neural networks which do not allow complex-valued computation or include physics-informed loss functions (24% – 41% decrease in the mean squared error of the density matrix).

papers.title: Physics-informed Klein--Gordon scattering from a tanh--exponential step in the spin-0 Duffin--Kemmer--Petiau sector
papers.abstract: We use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to compute how a spin-0 Duffin--Kemmer--Petiau boson scatters from the smooth electrostatic step \(V(x)=a\exp[\tanh(bx)]\). We first test both real basis fields and their derivatives against exact solutions for the simpler step \(V_{\mathrm{cal}}(x)=a\tanh(bx)\). On an independent spatial grid all four relative \(L^2\) errors are below \(6\times10^{-6}\). For the exponential step, we train two real networks to obtain independent solutions of the wave equation. At fixed energy, mass and potential, we combine these solutions and vary the complex reflection amplitude \(B\) after training to select the physical scattering state. The resulting field gives the reflection and transmission coefficients. In the Klein regime the reflected charge flux exceeds the incident flux, and the transmitted charge flux is negative. At \((E,a,b,m)=(5,5,3,1)\), the complex field agrees with an independent DOP853 integration to a relative \(L^2\) error of \(\EfiveProfileLtwo\). An energy sweep covers 32 cases. A second sweep covers 254 parameter combinations, with 29 shared and 225 additional cases, giving 257 distinct configurations. In the second sweep, the maximum absolute errors of the matched reflection and transmission coefficients are \(1.93\times10^{-4}\) and \(2.59\times10^{-4}\), respectively. Where the field decays on the right, a separate neural fit incorporates that decay to resolve the small tail. The trained solutions can be reused. New spatial coordinates require only network evaluation, and changing a trial \(B\) on an already sampled grid requires only a linear combination. For a query of the field and its derivative at 1001 new coordinates with \(E=8\), the stored DOP853 solution was faster to evaluate than the trained PINN (\(\QueryDense\) versus \(\QueryPinn\) ms). Both reused the solution already obtained. A fresh DOP853 integration and evaluation took \(\QueryOde\) ms.

papers.title: Prediction of Minimum Miscibility Pressure in CO2–Oil Systems Using Thermodynamic Bounds and Monotonic Gradient Constraints
papers.abstract: Minimum miscibility pressure (MMP) is a key design parameter for CO2-enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR) and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) projects. Although existing machine-learning models can capture the complex nonlinear relationships between fluid composition and MMP, their training processes remain predominantly data-driven, making them susceptible to locally non-physical responses in regions characterized by sparse samples or uneven compositional coverage. To address this limitation, this study develops a physics-informed neural network (PINN) incorporating thermodynamic priors. Based on 664 literature-derived samples, 11 predefined input variables covering injection-gas composition, crude-oil composition, and reservoir temperature are employed. Using a residual deep neural network (DNN) as the backbone, the modified Li empirical correlation is reformulated as a soft constraint with a tolerance interval to bound predictions within a macroscopically reasonable range. Meanwhile, automatic-differentiation-based monotonicity gradient penalties are imposed on eight variables with well-established physical response directions to suppress locally non-physical behavior. A progressive dynamic weight scheduling strategy is further introduced to enable a gradual transition from data-fitting dominance to the synergistic optimization of data and physical constraints. Under a nested evaluation framework combining five outer random splits with five-fold inner cross-validation, the proposed model is compared with Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost, CatBoost, Stacking, and an isomorphic purely data-driven DNN. The results demonstrate that the proposed PINN achieves the best overall performance, with an R2 of 0.9507 ± 0.0127 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.718 ± 0.530 MPa. Gradient-direction, partial dependence, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses indicate that the model generally preserves physically reasonable response patterns within its applicability domain (AD). The AD coverage rates for the training and test sets reach 96.3 and 95.2%, respectively. The proposed method provides a reference for the rapid and reliable estimation of MMP under compositionally complex injection-gas conditions.

papers.title: Mechanical property enhancement of laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing – AlSi10Mg parts with aging and hot isostatic pressing processes: Mechanical considerations
papers.abstract: In this work, the influence of post-treatment on the physical and mechanical properties of AlSi10Mg processed by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) on an EOS M 290 machine in three build orientations (0°, 45° and 90°) was analyzed quantitatively. The post-treatments comprised solution treatment (530 °C/2 h, water quenching) followed by natural aging (T4 temper) or by artificial aging at 150, 175 or 200 °C for 2 h (T6 temper), as well as hot isostatic pressing (HIP; 530 °C, 100 MPa, 2 h) and HIP followed by T6 aging at 175 °C (HIP + T6). Density measurements, Vickers hardness (HV0.2) tests, tensile tests, impulse excitation measurements of Young's modulus and fractography were carried out. The as-fabricated (AF) state showed the highest strength (ultimate tensile strength 474–506 MPa, yield strength 237–287 MPa) but the lowest elongation (≈6–10%) and a relative density of 97.6–98.9%. Solution treatment and aging decreased the strength by 35–40% and increased the elongation to ≈12–22%, but did not affect the porosity; aging at 175 °C gave the best T6 properties. HIP increased the relative density to 99.1–99.7% but halved the hardness, whereas HIP + T6 combined a relative density of 99.8–99.96% with ≈75–90% of the AF hardness, a tensile strength of ≈295–325 MPa and an elongation of ≈10–12.5%, and reduced the orientation-related difference in density from 1.24 to 0.14 percentage points. The findings of this comprehensive parametric study indicate that HIP + T6 provides the optimal combination of properties for meeting the mechanical requirements of industrial applications.

papers.title: Predictive modeling of convective heat transfer in nanofluid flow heat exchangers via hybrid machine learning frameworks
papers.abstract: In power generation, chemical processing, vehicle cooling, and renewable energy applications, heat exchangers are essential components but are constrained by the inability to use conventional working fluids with their limited heat-transfer capabilities. Convection heat transfer enhancement can be significantly obtained by the use of nanofluids containing nanometre size particles suspended in a base fluid, but it is a function of the interacting physical mechanisms and the physical ones are nonlinear, so classical empirical correlations may not be accurate out of the narrow parameter regions. This study investigates the ability of machine learning to accurately, generally and with quantified uncertainty predict convective heat transfer within nanofluid heat exchangers, and presents four hybrid machine-learning frameworks that address this question. The random forest combined with adaptive boosting, gradient boosting tuned with Bayesian optimization, support vector regression tuned with a genetic algorithm, and a stacking ensemble that fused predictions of a neural network, support vector and gradient boosting with ridge regression, all with feature selection and uncertainty interval calculation using a dropout-based method, from a unified database of over 1200 experimental records, which were acquired for six nanoparticle types, three base fluids, and three exchanger geometries. Stacking ensemble prediction error was reduced by approximately 75% compared with the best classical correlation and the coefficient of determination and the root-mean-square error were 0.978 and 4.8, respectively, covering 93–94% of the withheld experimental measurements in the uncertainty intervals. In a counter-flow double-pipe exchanger, the heat-transfer coefficient improvements of the alumina-water and copper-oxide-water nanofluids were 32 and 38% respectively at 1% volume fraction of nano particles, and the overall performance indices of the two ranged from 1.05 to 1.23 confirmed that the heat-transfer gain outweighed the pumping penalty.In contrast to previous work, which uses point predictions from a single learning algorithm trained on limited amounts of data, this work uses complementary learning algorithms, optimized uncertainty quantification and validation using data from an independent facility. The framework provides engineers with a quick and accurate data-based tool for the preliminary design and optimization of nanofluid heat exchangers to significantly decrease the amount of expensive experiments or high-fidelity simulations required during the initial design phase.

papers.title: A Controlled Evaluation of a Chebyshev-Coefficient Physics-Informed Neural Network for the Allen–Cahn Equation
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that output spectral coefficients have exact spatial derivatives. We evaluate a Chebyshev-coefficient PINN for the one-dimensional Allen–Cahn equation with Neumann conditions (four benchmarks, five seeds). Baselines are a classical solver, a reaction-only model, matched space–time PINNs, and a non-neural polynomial-in-time control with the same loss. An exact Neumann basis is needed: a soft penalty fails at large mode numbers, even with three standard remedies. On the diffusion-active benchmark, the network is not significantly more accurate than an exact-boundary space–time PINN, and 3.4 times less accurate after L-BFGS. With enough modes, the non-neural control beats every network at a fraction of the cost and solves an interface benchmark on which all globally trained PINNs fail. Symmetries enter through the output basis and hold exactly: even or odd Chebyshev modes and tied cosine coefficients halve the outputs but fail for symmetry-breaking data. An energy identity bounds the energy growth of any trial function by its residual. Coefficient networks trained globally without causal weights satisfy a sufficient condition for monotone energy; an energy penalty is unnecessary. Joint estimation of the interface parameter depends on the starting value, and the loss is smallest below the true value.

papers.title: Jumping Robots for Lunar Surface Exploration: Mechanisms, Motion Control, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Jumping can complement continuous driving by extending access across local obstacles and terrain gaps during lunar exploration. This review examines how jumping robots generate takeoff and coordinate flight, landing, and recovery. It compares leg and linkage mechanisms, structural deformation, internal mass motion, and propulsive takeoff, with examples including LEV-1, SpaceBok, and Salto-1P. Trajectory optimization, model predictive control, and reinforcement learning are considered according to the motion phases and control actions they address. The comparison identifies two connected design issues. The takeoff mechanism determines the forces available for subsequent motion, while landing and recovery determine whether an isolated jump can become sustained mobility. Reported heights, distances, and repetition results are interpreted together with gravity, external support, power supply, and validation conditions. These distinctions prevent terrestrial records or constrained tests from being treated as evidence of lunar readiness. The review therefore links mechanism and control choices to task requirements and identifies coordinated design, terrain-aware feedback, and integrated validation as priorities for lunar applications.

papers.title: Multi-phase degradation modelling: a review of model structures, statistical inference, and decision support
papers.abstract: Degradation analysis provides an important basis for reliability assessment, remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, and maintenance decision-making. However, many engineering systems exhibit distinct degradation phases due to changes in operating conditions or underlying degradation mechanisms. Ignoring such phase transitions may lead to inaccurate lifetime predictions and inappropriate maintenance decisions. This paper presents a systematic review of multi-phase degradation analysis. We first introduce the basic concepts and characteristics of multi-phase degradation, and then summarize major modelling approaches, including general path models and stochastic process models. We further discuss inference and identification issues, including parameter estimation and change-point detection, as well as downstream applications in RUL prediction and maintenance optimization. Finally, open challenges and future directions are discussed in terms of mechanism-informed modelling, uncertainty quantification, generalizable prediction, and artificial-intelligence-enabled phase-aware degradation analysis.

papers.abstract: This article critically examines the optimistic discourse that, since Law No. 13,415/2017 and the Brazilian National Common Curricular Base (BNCC), has presented high school reform as an opportunity to renew Physics education. This discourse is commonly organized around five axes: curricular flexibility, technological education, “teacher education 4.0,” active student participation, and formative assessment. The value of each of these dimensions is acknowledged. However, this article argues that the narrative of opportunity tends to treat optimism as a premise rather than as the outcome of an investigation: it asserts effectiveness without method or data, overlooks the political and regulatory context of the reform, relies on generic sources, and engages insufficiently with Physics as a specific disciplinary field. The analysis draws on Brazilian literature on the reform and Physics education, as well as international empirical studies on active learning, simulations, and feedback. Finally, it outlines ways to give the debate greater theoretical and empirical depth.

papers.title: An Integrated Machine Learning Framework for Wind Speed Forecasting and Energy Estimation with Cross-Site Evaluation
papers.abstract: Wind speed (WS) and wind energy (WE) prediction are key to the proper operation of a power system (PS) and the integration of wind turbines. Existing research, however, has primarily focused on prediction accuracy and feature engineering. Model interpretability, statistical validation, energy evaluation, uncertainty quantification, and cross-site validation within a single framework remain understudied. This research introduces an integrated machine learning (ML) framework that combines automated data processing, multidirectional temporal feature engineering, model benchmarking, WE evaluation, statistical validation, explainable prediction, uncertainty analysis, and cross-site estimation. This study also translates forecast errors into wind power density and turbine-energy terms and tests the trained model at independent stations. This research tests five predictive models on 26,304 hourly WS observations: Linear Regression (LR), gradient boosting (GB), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with Attention, Convolutional Neural Network–Gated Recurrent Unit (CNN–GRU) hybrid, and Random Forest (RF). The optimal predictive performance was obtained by GB, with R2 = 0.8026, RMSE = 4.3303 km/h, and MAE = 3.1574 km/h. Shapley additive exPlanations (SHAP) investigation revealed that short-term lagged WS parameters were the most significant predictors and presented a representation of the significance of the temporal persistence in forecasting WS. For validation, the trained GB model used for Nowra was applied to two different geographic stations. It reaches R2 = 0.8353, RMSE = 3.82 km/h and MAE = 2.75 km/h at coastal Ballina Airport (BA) (about 735 km north) and R2 = 0.6944 and RMSE = 4.36 km/h at inland Deniliquin Airport (about 515 km west), where persistence remains stronger. The central 95% range of the test errors spans −7.32 to +8.23 km/h. The suggested framework, which integrates predictive modelling, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, statistical validation, energy-oriented evaluation, and cross-site estimation, constitutes a thorough framework of reliable short-term WS forecasting and operational decision-making for WE.

papers.abstract: Fourier features can improve the representation of oscillatory signals in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), but their accuracy advantage may change with the underlying nonlinear dynamics. We compare a conventional PINN and a three-branch multi-scale Fourier-feature PINN (MFPINN) for the conservative nonlinear pendulum at five initial amplitudes between 0.1 and 3.0 rad. Both models are assessed against an adaptive Runge–Kutta reference on a fixed dimensionless time interval. The reported relative L2 errors vary by orders of magnitude across amplitudes. MFPINN is more accurate in three cases, whereas the conventional PINN is more accurate in two, including the near-separatrix case. A conservation penalty is used at the largest amplitude, but its effect cannot be separated from changes in training effort. These findings establish an amplitude-resolved numerical benchmark and show why model capacity, training reproducibility and dynamical regime must be controlled before attributing accuracy gains to Fourier features or energy constraints. The results are relevant to the reliability assessment of model-based vibration reconstruction, rather than a claim of experimental sensor validation.

papers.title: First evaluation of a woven tissue-engineered vascular graft made of cell-assembled extracellular matrix in an allogeneic large animal model.
papers.abstract: Commercial vascular grafts remain limited by poor biological integration, chronic inflammation, susceptibility to infection, and the inability to remodel into living tissue. Our research group has developed a biological material synthesized by dermal human fibroblasts, known as Cell-Assembled extracellular Matrix (CAM). This study presents the first use of CAM-based constructs in an allogeneic large animal model. Woven tissue-engineered vascular grafts (wTEVGs) were produced on a circular loom using longitudinal ribbons and a circumferential thread made of CAM produced by ovine dermal fibroblasts. In vitro characterization of the wTEVGs (inner diameter of 4.3 mm) revealed supraphysiological mechanical properties with a suture retention strength of 7.3 ± 2.1 N and a burst pressure of 4800 ± 760 mmHg. Carotid interposition grafting of the wTEVG in sheep was performed using standard techniques and instruments without complications. No leakage was observed at the anastomosis or through the wall upon blood flow restoration. All grafts were patent at four weeks, with no evidence of dilation or perigraft seroma, as determined by angiography and echography. A neotissue composed of collagen and containing smooth muscle and endothelial cells was visible at each extremity of the inner graft surface after 4 weeks. Furthermore, histological analysis showed no evidence of foreign-body response at four weeks and the integration of the graft with the native tissue. This study demonstrates, for the first time, that allogeneic CAM-based wTEVGs can safely sustain arterial circulation in a large-animal model while supporting early host-mediated luminal neotissue formation, highlighting their potential as vascular substitutes. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Current tissue-engineered vascular grafts often rely on synthetic scaffolds, decellularized tissues, or complex bioreactor-based manufacturing, limiting their translational potential. Here, we introduce a fundamentally different biofabrication strategy based on woven textiles produced entirely from Cell-Assembled extracellular Matrix, enabling the fabrication of fully biological, scaffold-free vascular grafts. We demonstrate that these grafts possess suitable mechanical properties for arterial implantation and support rapid constructive remodeling, partial endothelialization at a very short-term post-implantation time, and favorable hemodynamic adaptation in an allogeneic large-animal model. This work establishes biological textiles as a versatile platform for engineering load-bearing regenerative implants, offering new opportunities for cardiovascular tissue engineering and regenerative biomaterials.

papers.title: Controversies in Pterygoid Implantology
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pterygoid implant placement represents a contemporary therapeutic approach to the management of severe posterior maxillary atrophy. In addition to providing stable implant anchorage in the pterygomaxillary region, this technique may offer a less invasive alternative to certain augmentation procedures, such as maxillary sinus floor elevation and zygomatic implant placement. The choice of treatment approach depends on the individual clinical condition, anatomical circumstances, and the clinician’s assessment. Contemporary implant treatment planning aims to eliminate the need for a cantilever in the posterior maxilla. AIM: The aim of this lecture is to discuss the clinical challenges, anatomical limitations, and controversies associated with the planning and placement of pterygoid implants, with particular emphasis on their role in achieving long-term stability of implant-supported prosthetic reconstructions in edentulous maxillae. LECTURE CONTENT: Particular attention will be given to the importance of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) as the basis for preoperative planning of pterygoid implant placement. The assessment will include the volume of the maxillary tuberosity, the angulation of the pterygoid processes in relation to the alveolar ridge, and the anatomical characteristics of the medial pterygoid process as reference parameters for determining the implant trajectory. The clinical aspects of placing the so-called “blind” pterygoid implant will also be presented. During this procedure, the deep portion of the surgical preparation is not directly visualized. Consequently, successful placement requires detailed anatomical knowledge, precise spatial orientation, and a well-developed tactile sense. Palpatory identification of the pterygoid hamulus (hamulus pterygoideus) and the distal aspect of the maxillary tuberosity provides additional clinical guidance during the procedure. The pterygomaxillary region is characterized by considerable anatomical variations; therefore, successful implant placement requires appropriate training, clinical experience, and an individualized approach. The lecture will address the possibilities of achieving cortical anchorage in the pterygoid process, the role of implant geometry and design, and the factors influencing primary stability and osseointegration. Particular attention will be given to the concept of the pterygoid implant as a “rescue implant”, representing an important therapeutic option for providing posterior implant support and reducing or eliminating cantilevers in patients with complete maxillary edentulism. CONCLUSION: Pterygoid implantology represents an important therapeutic option for the reconstruction of the atrophic posterior maxilla. Its predictability depends on accurate radiological planning, knowledge of anatomical variations, clinical expertise, and appropriate implant system selection. Pterygoid implants play a significant role in achieving stable posterior support and long-term functionality of implant-supported prosthetic reconstructions.

papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Guided implant surgery represents a contemporary approach to implant-prosthetic rehabilitation, enabling more accurate and predictable dental implant placement through digital planning and the use of surgical guides. Its application is particularly relevant in pterygoid implant placement, which represents a therapeutic option for the rehabilitation of the atrophic posterior maxilla and may, in selected clinical cases, eliminate the need for additional augmentation procedures. AIM: The aim of this lecture is to present the applications and clinical significance of surgical guides in pterygoid implant placement, with particular emphasis on digital planning, surgical accuracy, appropriate patient selection, and the prevention of potential complications. LECTURE CONTENT: The anatomical characteristics of the pterygomaxillary region and the importance of detailed preoperative assessment in pterygoid implant planning will be discussed. Particular attention will be given to cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) analysis, its integration with intraoral scans, and the three-dimensional determination of the optimal implant position, angulation, and length. The principles of designing and applying static surgical guides, their role in accurately transferring the virtual plan to the clinical setting, and their limitations will be presented. Furthermore, factors affecting procedural safety will be addressed, including control of the surgical trajectory, protection of adjacent anatomical structures, achievement of primary stability, and selection of an appropriate prosthetic concept. CONCLUSION: The use of surgical guides, combined with digital planning and appropriate preventive protocols, may contribute to greater accuracy and predictability in pterygoid implant placement. However, treatment success depends on individual anatomical characteristics, appropriate patient selection, surgical expertise, and long-term maintenance of peri-implant tissues.

papers.title: Cross-Technique Explainability Agreement Analysis for Machine Learning-Based Forest Fire Burned Area Modeling
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of forest fire burned area is essential for mitigating ecological degradation, economic losses, and risks to human life. Although machine learning (ML) models have shown considerable potential for wildfire prediction, their practical adoption remains limited by insufficient interpretability and limited assessment of explanation consistency across complementary XAI methods. This study proposes an integrated explainable machine learning framework for forest fire burned area modeling using the publicly available UCI Forest Fires dataset. Eight regression algorithms were comparatively evaluated, followed by Bayesian hyperparameter optimization using Scikit-Optimize (skopt) with Gaussian Process regression to identify the optimal predictive model. The optimized Extra Trees regressor achieved the comparatively best performance among the evaluated models with a 10-fold cross-validated coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.0061 ± 0.0295 (RMSE: 1.3740 ± 0.1857, MAE: 1.1332 ± 0.1320). To improve model transparency, SHAP, Permutation Feature Importance (PFI), Partial Dependence Plots (PDP), Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE), LIME, and a surrogate decision tree were employed to provide complementary global and local explanations. PDP and ICE analyses revealed near-monotonic positive marginal effects for temperature and December, with narrow ICE curve dispersion indicating homogenous instance-level response patterns across the dataset. Furthermore, a cross-technique explainability agreement analysis was introduced using Spearman rank correlation, Kendall's Tau, Jaccard similarity, and consensus-based feature analysis to quantitatively evaluate the consistency of explanations across multiple XAI methods. The proposed analysis demonstrated exceptionally strong cross-technique agreement, achieving a Spearman rank correlation of 0.9823 (95% CI: [0.9612, 0.9918]), Kendall's Tau of 0.9145 (95% CI: [0.8745, 0.9390]), and a Jaccard similarity index of 1.000 between the global SHAP and PFI feature rankings, while identifying September, December, March, and temperature as consistently influential predictors within the fitted model's decision function, with September, December, and higher temperatures exerting positive influences that increase predicted burned area, whereas March conditions exert a negative influence that decreases predicted burned area. Overall, the proposed framework provides a systematic approach for analyzing model behavior and evaluating explanation agreement across multiple complementary XAI techniques on a challenging forest fire burned area benchmark dataset.

papers.title: A Patient-Specific Digital Twin Framework for Personalized Healthcare using Hybrid Artificial Intelligence and Physiological Simulation
papers.abstract: Personalized healthcare requires clinical decisions that account for differences between individuals rather than relying only on population averages. A patient-specific digital twin (PSDT) is a computational representation of an individual that can be updated using clinical observations and used to explore plausible health trajectories. This paper proposes a conceptual hybrid framework that combines artificial intelligence (AI) with physiological simulation to support patient-level monitoring, risk forecasting, and treatment “what-if” analysis. The framework integrates electronic health records, laboratory results, medical imaging, physiological signals, and wearable data through a quality-control and temporal-alignment layer. Machine-learning models extract patterns from heterogeneous data, while mechanistic or reduced-order simulators represent selected physiological processes. A personalization loop calibrates twin parameters as new observations arrive and communicates uncertainty alongside predictions. The output is designed as clinician-supervised decision support, not autonomous diagnosis or treatment. The paper describes the architecture, workflow, candidate evaluation protocol, application scenarios, and governance requirements. As a conceptual study, it does not report patient experiments or measured clinical performance; prospective validation is identified as necessary before clinical use.

papers.title: Physics-guided surrogate modeling of injection-driven transport in LLZO solid electrolytes: contact-dependent injection and space-charge effects
papers.abstract: Understanding injection-driven current in solid electrolytes is important for assessing the reliability of all-solid-state batteries. This study investigates charge transport in Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂ (LLZO) using a bipolar charge transport (BCT) model coupled with a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) surrogate. The model employs extracting contacts and a thermionic-emission-diffusion injection boundary condition. The associated barrier heights and contact-state densities are assumed rather than calibrated, and the model represents only excess injected carriers on top of a neutral background, not the intrinsic Li⁺ population of LLZO. On an independent hold-out set of 60 new BCT simulations, 39 admissible cases are retained. The GPR reproduces the numerical model with R² = 0.99998, an RMSE of 0.0023 decades and a median absolute relative error of 0.27%, but does not extrapolate reliably in voltage. In batch evaluation, the prediction cost is approximately 6.1 µs per point, compared with 16.3 s per BCT run. The current density of the admissible simulations spans approximately 6 × 10⁻⁶ to 1.5 × 10⁻³ A·m⁻². Global sensitivity analysis over the full prescribed parameter space gives total Sobol indices of 0.82 for lithium-ion mobility and 0.14 for applied voltage, while all trap-related indices are below 10⁻⁴. These indices characterize the surrogate over the full parameter space and are not restricted to admissible BCT configurations. In an extended trap-stress test, the maximum absolute relative current change among admissible non-reference configurations is 5.14%. For the reference contact, the local current-voltage exponent remains between 1.25 and 1.29, whereas the fitted exponent ranges from 1.16 to 1.99 across eight assumed contact configurations with admissible voltages, out of nine tested. This indicates that the transport regime depends on the assumed interfacial injection conditions, rather than on a universal transition voltage. Direct simulations in a device-like voltage range of 0.5–5 V yield seven admissible cases out of 18, with current densities between 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ and 7.2 × 10⁻⁶ A·m⁻². These findings are model-dependent numerical predictions, not experimental validation of LLZO transport, and further experimental investigation is required.

papers.title: A two-network audit shows when conformal prediction intervals for solar irradiance forecasts remain valid at newly commissioned stations
papers.abstract: A newly commissioned solar site needs trustworthy probabilistic forecasts immediately, yet conformal prediction’s coverage guarantee assumes local calibration data that a new site lacks. We audit this cold-start gap with leave-one-station-out experiments on two networks, 13 continental-US NOAA stations (donors 200–3700 km apart) and 28 PV-Live stations (donors 10–240 km apart), with four forecasters and four horizons (15 min to 6 h). Pooled-donor calibration with zero local data is near-nominal on average but not per station: at 6 h, only 54–69% of station-years stay within ± 2% points. Local calibration restores validity at horizons up to 1 h for three of four forecasters after a median 21–136 days of local data; a prospective self-certification rule reproduces this limit. At 3–6 h, most station-years never sustain coverage within ± 1% point through 182 days, a failure shared by dense donors and even a full local year, consistent with temporal drift. Delayed-feedback donor-seeded adaptive conformal inference holds every station’s marginal coverage near nominal by construction, at a Winkler-score cost of at most about 2% on identical evaluation steps for the learned forecasters, with occasional infinite intervals and a 30–60-day transient. We distill a deployment protocol for new solar sites.

papers.title: EvoSeq: A Eukaryotic Sequence‐Function Profiling Platform for AI‐Guided Engineering of Genome‐Editing Enzymes
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping protein engineering, yet progress remains constrained by the limited availability of scalable, normalized sequence-activity datasets and experimental benchmarks. Reported here is Evolution by Sequencing (EvoSeq), a sequencing-based profiling platform for genome-editing enzymes that links each variant to a reporter sequence change, enabling activity and variant sequence to be quantified together by next-generation sequencing. Representative sequencing-assisted workflows either require separate functional assays or were performed in bacteria. EvoSeq performs sequence-activity profiling in eukaryotic yeast system with reduced background by up to 95-fold compared to bacterial system, positioning EvoSeq as a pooled eukaryotic alternative to workflows that require separate functional assays and to approaches demonstrated primarily in bacteria. Application to adenine base editor evolution identifies variants with 1.4-fold higher on-target activity at a HBG gene target and threefold lower off-target editing at PCSK9 after mRNA-lipid nanoparticle validation in HepG2 cells. An intron-embedded homologous-recombination recording strategy further enables direct evolution of the large Cas12i nuclease CasY7 and supports active learning, increasing the hit rate of model-nominated mutational windows compared with manual selection. EvoSeq therefore provides an experimental benchmarking method for AI-guided protein-design algorithms and AI-compatible sequence-activity profiling platform for engineering genome editors in eukaryotic cells.

papers.title: Center–Environment Feature Engineering for Interpretable and Data-Efficient Machine Learning in Catalyst Discovery
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) offers a novel paradigm for accelerating catalyst discovery; however, model accuracy, generalizability, and interpretability depend critically on catalyst representation. In contrast to global graph-based representations, the Center–Environment (CE) framework incorporates explicit physical priors by designating property-relevant atoms or sites as centers and influential neighboring atoms as their environments. Feature vectors are constructed through linear combinations of intrinsic elementary attributes weighted by inverse Center–Environment distances, thereby encoding coupled local chemical and structural information. This mini-review examines the principles, methodological evolution, and catalytic applications of CE and Surface Center–Environment (SCE) models, emphasizing how flexible definitions of centers and environments, together with the assembly of elemental properties, establish an active-site-oriented inductive bias. CE-based ML was first applied in 2020 to assess the stability of spinel oxides. Developed concurrently for the oxygen-evolution reaction (OER) on perovskite oxide surfaces, SCE was subsequently extended to hydrocarbon precursor adsorption and early-stage nanocarbon growth on alloy catalysts. CE features have also enabled deep-transfer learning across spinel and perovskite structures. Furthermore, CE-based ML has been integrated with SHAP interpretation, physical descriptors, hierarchical screening, and experimental validation to establish a closed-loop workflow for spinel OER catalyst discovery. Comparisons with composition-based features, Voronoi representations, and graph neural networks (GNNs) highlight the strengths of CE. Reported studies show that CE balances data efficiency and interpretability on small- to medium-sized first-principles datasets through a predefined attention mechanism that reflects the influence of the local environment on an active site. However, current implementations are constrained by the compression of many-body information and limited automation of feature construction and discovery workflows. Promising directions include automated construction of high-dimensional CE representations incorporating many-body interactions, hybrid CE–GNN models, uncertainty-guided active learning, and closed-loop integration of density functional theory, ML, and experiments under realistic reaction conditions.

papers.title: Design and Control of WLR‐4P: A Lightweight Wheel‐Bipedal Robot With Obstacle Crossing Ability and Complex Terrain Adaptability
papers.abstract: Designing lightweight structures with high power‐to‐weight ratios and developing robust multi‐contact motion control are critical for enhancing the mobility and environmental adaptability of wheel‐legged mobile robots. This work presents WLR‐4P, a 40‐kg wheel‐bipedal robot featuring substantial lightweight hardware iteration, a compact onboard hydraulic system, and a novel hierarchical control framework. Compared with its predecessor, WLR‐3P, WLR‐4P achieves a 50% reduction in total mass while retaining comparable standing dimensions. The hydraulic drive unit (HDU) has a calculated ideal peak hydraulic power density of 6.98 kW/kg at 21 MPa. The three‐layer control paradigm decouples long‐horizon trajectory optimization, MPC‐based disturbance rejection, and rolling‐constrained inverse kinematics to realize unified rolling, obstacle‐traversal, and jumping locomotion. Prototype tests across flat ground, structured obstacles, and natural outdoor terrains show improved velocity‐tracking performance relative to the in‐house LQR engineering baseline. Four commanded vertical‐jumping trials are completed without falling, with a mean landing‐window peak pelvis pitch of 0.1966 rad. Note that the reported 0.60‐m value represents a commanded upper‐CoM reference excursion rather than an independently measured jump height. This study validates the prototype‐level feasibility of the integrated hardware‐software system and provides a reference for the design of high performance hydraulic wheel‐biped robots.
